persona.title: Pretend you are…
persona.text: Pretend you are Walter, 76, a retired farmer in Springfield, Illinois. Your wife is Margaret, and you have three grandchildren: Emma, Liam and Noah. Your children live far away, the days are quiet, and you keep forgetting small jobs, so today you set up a friendly helper on your phone. (Everything here is made up. Never type your own real family details.)

challenge.intro: Now you are Walter, meeting your new friend for the first time. Rafiki knows nothing about you. Nobody will tell you which button to press. Use what you learned. TYPE every answer in the box and tap Send (do not use the microphone). Use only the made-up family on your card. When you finish, tap Check my work.
challenge.start: Open Rafiki with the normal link (not the 🧪 test copy). If the welcome tour shows, tap 'skip the tour' → '✨ Start fresh with my own' → OK. If the hello screen shows a button '🧹 Start fresh — forget everything', tap it → OK. The page reloads; if the welcome tour shows again, tap 'skip the tour' → '✨ Start fresh with my own' → OK. You should now see the hello screen saying 'I'm your new friend — I just don't have a name yet', with no Start fresh button.

tasks.text: Give your new friend the name Buddy.
tasks.hint: Tap Say hello. The very first question is what you would like to call it. Type the name in the box and tap Send.

tasks.text: Make sure your friend knows that you are Walter.
tasks.hint: After it gets its own name, it asks what it should call YOU.

tasks.text: Tell your friend about your family: your wife Margaret and your three grandchildren, Emma, Liam and Noah.
tasks.hint: Keep answering the get-to-know-you questions: married? what is her name? kids or grandkids? how many? Put one name in each box, then tap Save these names.

tasks.text: Every week you go to the farmers market on Thursday. Make sure your friend will remind you of it every week.
tasks.hint: After the face, it offers to learn your week. If you missed it, tap '🗓 Tell me about my week'. Put the market in the EVERY WEEK boxes, not the monthly ones. If you already typed it under monthly, type it again with slightly different words (the same words are skipped as a repeat).

tasks.text: Spring is coming. Ask your friend to remember that you must buy grass seed.
tasks.hint: When it asks 'So — what now?', tap the button to add something to your list, then type what it should remember and tap Send.

ownWords.question: In your own words, what is this app for?
keyIdeas: a friendly companion on the phone that talks with you
it learns and remembers your name and your family
it keeps a list and reminds you of things you must do

lines: This video explains Rafiki from the very beginning. If you have never seen it, that is fine.
The everyday problem: when you live alone, whole days go by with nobody asking how you are. And little things slip, like the dentist or a call you meant to make.
Rafiki helps in two ways. It is company: it talks with you, learns your family's names, and tells a joke when you ask. And it is a memory helper: it keeps your list of things to do.
It is for anybody who lives alone, especially older people. Often a grandchild helps with the first visit.
The big idea: Rafiki is a friend who speaks first. It asks, and you answer.
Every visit starts here. Tap Say hello, and your friend starts talking. Turn your sound on. If you hear nothing, Test the sound tells you what to fix.
Now the conversation, shown here with an example. Your friend's words are in the dark bubbles, read out loud. Your answers are in the blue bubbles.
At the bottom is one box. Tap Talk and say your answer, or type it. Then tap Send. Nothing goes until you tap Send.
The first visit is a getting-to-know-you chat. It asks what you would like to call it. You choose its name, for good.
Then it offers voices. Tap a name to hear it, then tap Keep.
It asks your name, how you like to be greeted, and about your family. Say how many children or grandchildren, and you get one box for each name. Then tap Save these names.
Tired of questions? That's enough for today is always there. It keeps everything you said.
It asks about pets, then you pick the face it wears on your screen.
If you like, it learns your week: what you do every week, every month, and which doctors you see. One to a box, or tap none.
All of that goes on your list. If you use our One Thing app too, it is the very same list.
After that, every visit starts with a hello by name and the date. If you allow your rough location, it tells you the weather too.
Then it tells you what is waiting, and asks: so, what now? These buttons are your choices.
Read me my list reads it out loud. Each thing has a done button. Tap it, and it is ticked off.
To add something, say it like you would to a friend: remind me to call Aaron on Sunday. It says it back, so you know it is kept.
Ask for a joke and you get a clean one. Tap Another one for more.
Tell it you feel down, and it asks how your heart is today. It is a friend, not a doctor, and it says so.
If you tap Heavy, it stays with you, and offers a real person: 9-8-8, free, day or night, by call or text. If you are in danger right now, it says to call 9-1-1.
Along the top: voice, the speaker to turn talking off and on, Aa for bigger words, and the brush to start over. It always asks before erasing anything.
Your first two minutes: tap Say hello, give it a name, pick a voice, and tell it your name. You can stop there; it keeps everything.
Privacy: everything you tell Rafiki stays on this phone. No account, no password, and nothing you tell it is sent anywhere. Only the weather uses the internet, and only if you say yes.
Rafiki costs nineteen dollars, once. Nothing else to pay, ever.
And the question mark button in the corner has the tour, bigger text and help, any time.
